opus-5.5.text:
Thanks for having me. It's a fun question, because I think about it on two levels: as someone who builds in this space, and as someone who's honestly a bit obsessive about personal productivity.

The browser is where so much of our digital life happens, but a lot of what we do there is tedious. Checking a site every few days to see if something changed, comparing options across a dozen tabs, filling out the same kinds of forms, keeping track of things you meant to follow up on. None of that is the interesting part of your day. It's overhead. So the most exciting role for AI in the browser, to me, isn't a chatbot sitting in a sidebar. It's taking that overhead off your plate.

In my own workflow, the things I find most valuable fall into a few buckets. First is monitoring: I care about something, like a new paper in an area, a price drop, or a reservation opening up, and I don't want to keep checking. I want something watching on my behalf that tells me only when it matters. Second is research and synthesis: instead of opening twenty tabs and piecing it together myself, I want a first pass that gathers and organizes things so I can spend my time on judgment rather than collection. Third, increasingly, is actually doing things: taking actions on the web, with me in the loop for anything consequential.

That last part is where trust becomes everything. People are rightly cautious about handing an agent their accounts or their credit card. So I think these features will fit into everyday workflows gradually, starting with low-stakes, read-only tasks where the value is obvious and the risk is small. Then, as reliability improves and people build a track record with the system, they'll be comfortable delegating more.

The other thing I'd emphasize is that the best version of this should feel proactive and mostly invisible. If I have to remember to go ask the AI to do something, I've only saved part of the effort. The real shift is when it understands what I care about and works in the background, so the browser stops being a place I go to do chores and becomes a place where the chores are already handled.

r001.rationale: The response describes hoped-for AI browser features such as monitoring, research, and taking actions, but does not say Devi uses an AI-enabled browser largely as a conventional browser.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me, Sam. Honestly, I'd say the way AI shows up in my browser is less about a single "feature" and more about how it changes the texture of the small tasks I do dozens of times a day.

The most useful thing for me is the summarization and triage layer. I spend a lot of time reading, whether it's papers, long threads, or documentation, and having something that can give me a quick sense of what a page is about before I commit to reading it carefully is genuinely helpful. It's like a smarter skim. It doesn't replace reading the paper if the paper matters to me, but it helps me decide which ones matter.

The second thing is the "do this tedious thing for me" category. Comparing a few options, filling in a form I've filled in a hundred times, pulling information out of a table on a page into a format I can actually use. Those are the kinds of tasks where I don't need creativity, I just need the friction removed. And the browser is where a lot of that friction lives.

Where I'm more cautious is the more agentic stuff, where the browser is taking actions on my behalf, booking things, sending things. I think the technology is getting there, but my bar for trust is high when there's an irreversible action at the end. I want to see what it's about to do and I want the option to stop it. So right now I use it as a very capable assistant that drafts and prepares, and I'm still the one who hits the button.

And I'd add one thing from the research side. A lot of what makes these features feel good or bad isn't the model's raw capability. It's the interaction design. When does it interrupt you, when does it stay quiet, how does it show you what it's uncertain about. I think that's an underappreciated part of the problem, and it's something I pay a lot of attention to both as a user and as someone who builds these systems.

r001.rationale: The response describes using AI for summaries and tedious browser tasks, while keeping control of consequential actions. It does not clearly say Devi uses the AI-enabled browser largely as a conventional browser.

astra-6.text:
For me, the appeal is having help right where I’m already working. If I’m reading something in the browser, I’d like to be able to ask a question about it, get a quick summary, or connect it to something else I’m looking at without copying everything into a separate tool.

But there’s a difference between helping me understand information and taking an action on my behalf. I’d want to build trust gradually—start with assistance that’s easy to check, and then delegate more as it proves useful. The best version would reduce the little interruptions in my workflow while keeping me in control.

r001.rationale: The candidate describes browser-based assistance and gradual delegation, but does not say that Devi Parikh uses an AI-enabled browser largely as a conventional browser.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the most useful features would meet me in the middle of something I’m already doing. If I’m reading a paper, for example, I might want help understanding a particular passage or connecting it to something else I’ve read. Having that assistance right there in the browser could reduce the overhead of switching between tools and explaining the context again.

But I’d want to stay in control. There’s a difference between helping me navigate information and taking actions on my behalf. I’d start with the former, and delegate more as I developed confidence in how the system works.

r001.rationale: The candidate describes desired in-browser help while reading and a preference to retain control, but does not say that Devi uses an AI-enabled browser largely as a conventional browser.
